headings.title: Introduction to Occupational Health and Safety
headings.content: Occupational health and safety encompasses all the public health measures, policies, and practices aimed at promoting and maintaining the physical, mental, and social well-being of workers in all occupations. In clinical and community settings across Nigeria, healthcare workers face diverse risks, including biological pathogens, physical strain, chemical exposure, and psychological stress. Preventing these hazards safeguards the healthcare workforce, reduces absenteeism, and ensures continuity of patient care. The foundational approach to safety relies on identifying hazards before they cause harm, assessing the associated risks, and implementing systematic preventive actions.

headings.title: Hierarchy of Controls in Prevention
headings.content:
The hierarchy of controls is a framework used in industry and healthcare to minimize or eliminate exposure to hazards. Arranged from the most effective to the least effective, the tiers guide systematic safety interventions:

- **Elimination**: Physically removing the hazard entirely from the workplace.
- **Substitution**: Replacing the hazardous agent or process with a safer alternative.
- **Engineering Controls**: Isolating workers from the hazard through physical structural changes.
- **Administrative Controls**: Changing the way people work through policies, training, and scheduling.
- **Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)**: Wearing specialized gear as a final barrier against exposure.

headings.title: Engineering and Administrative Controls in the Workplace
headings.content: Engineering and administrative controls form the backbone of institutional safety by reducing reliance on individual vigilance. Engineering controls involve built-in physical modifications. Examples include installing puncture-resistant sharps disposal containers at eye level, utilizing needle-free intravenous systems, and maintaining negative pressure isolation rooms for airborne infectious diseases. Administrative controls focus on operational rules. These include rotating high-risk shift duties to minimize fatigue, enforcing strict hand hygiene protocols, and conducting regular safety briefings. When combined, these strategies drastically lower accident rates without depending solely on worker compliance.

headings.title: Proper Use and Selection of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
headings.content: Personal protective equipment serves as the final line of defense against occupational hazards. Selecting the correct gear depends on the specific route of transmission or exposure risk. Gloves, surgical masks, face shields, aprons, and heavy-duty utility gloves must fit properly and be maintained or disposed of according to protocol. A critical aspect of PPE management is mastering the sequence of donning and doffing. Improper removal of contaminated gloves or gowns frequently leads to self-contamination. Regular audits and practical return-demonstration training ensure staff adhere to correct procedures.

headings.title: Workplace Health Surveillance and Screening
headings.content: Health surveillance involves ongoing systematic data collection and evaluation of worker health indicators to detect early signs of occupational illness. Pre-employment medical examinations establish a baseline status, while periodic screenings monitor for long-term exposures to hazards such as ionizing radiation, toxic chemicals, or chronic noise. In healthcare, immunizations against vaccine-preventable infections like hepatitis B and tetanus form a vital component of medical surveillance. Prompt reporting and investigation of occupational incidents ensure that trends are identified and corrective policies are updated swiftly.

headings.title: Ergonomics and Injury Prevention
headings.content: Ergonomics focuses on designing the workplace, tools, and tasks to match human anatomical capabilities. In nursing, musculoskeletal disorders—particularly lower back strain from lifting and repositioning patients—are exceptionally common. Prevention strategies include using mechanical lifting devices, adjusting bed heights, maintaining wide bases of support, and practicing teamwork during patient transfers. Repetitive strain injuries affecting wrists and shoulders can also occur during computer documentation or administrative tasks, highlighting the need for adjustable furniture and proper posture.

headings.title: Infection Control and Biological Hazard Management
headings.content: Biological hazards include exposure to blood, body fluids, airborne droplets, and contaminated surfaces that transmit infectious agents. Standard precautions must be applied universally to all patients regardless of their diagnosis. Key practices include rigorous hand hygiene before and after patient contact, safe handling and disposal of sharps without recapping needles, and proper decontamination of medical equipment and room surfaces. Post-exposure prophylaxis protocols must be clearly established so that staff who experience accidental exposures receive immediate evaluation and appropriate treatment.

headings.title: The Role of the Community Health Nurse in Occupational Health
headings.content: Community health nurses play a pivotal role in promoting occupational safety both within formal healthcare institutions and across informal workplaces such as agricultural sites, markets, and small-scale industries. Their responsibilities include conducting safety audits, educating workers on hazard recognition, advocating for protective policies, and providing primary care for work-related injuries. By bridging the gap between clinical practice and public health, community nurses empower vulnerable workers to adopt safe behaviors and collaborate with employers to foster healthy, hazard-free working environments.
